title: Showing things with print
idea: A program is a list of instructions that Python follows from the top, one line at a time.
The instruction `print` shows something on the screen. Whatever you put inside the round brackets is what appears.
Words must sit inside quote marks. Quote marks tell Python: this is text, not an instruction. Numbers do not need quote marks.
symbols: show what is inside the brackets, then move to a new line
quote marks: everything between them is text
inside print, a comma puts a space between two things

example.caption: Watch the printed text grow on the right as each line runs. Press Next line to move one line at a time.

predict.why: Each print starts a new line. The quote marks are not shown, they only tell Python the thing is text. The comma adds one space.

title: Variables: names that hold values
idea: A variable is a name that holds a value, like a labelled box. You choose the name.
The single equals sign `=` means store. Python works out the right side first, then puts the answer in the name on the left.
You can change what a name holds later. The old value is thrown away.
symbols: store the value on the right into the name on the left

example.caption: Look at the trace table. Each row shows the names and what they hold after the line before it has run.
example.code:
apples = 3
oranges = 4
total = apples + oranges
apples = 10
print(total)
print(apples)

predict.why: `y` was worked out when x held 5, so y became 7. Changing x later does not change y.

title: One equals sign or two
idea: `=` stores a value. `==` asks a question: are these two things equal. The answer is `True` or `False`.
Mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes. Say it aloud: one equals means put it in, two equals means is it the same.
`!=` asks the opposite question: are these different. `<` means less than and `>` means greater than.
symbols: store a value in a name
ask: are these equal. Gives True or False
the two answers to a yes or no question

example.caption: Notice that the stored answers are True or False, not words.
example.code:
a = 6
b = 6
same = a == b
different = a != b
bigger = a > 10
print(same)
print(different)
print(bigger)

predict.why: n holds 4, so asking n == 4 gives True. Asking n == 5 gives False.

title: The remainder with %
idea: The symbol `%` gives the remainder after dividing. 7 % 3 is 1, because 3 goes into 7 two times (that is 6) and 1 is left over.
If a number divides exactly, the remainder is 0. So `n % 2 == 0` is the standard way to ask: is n even.
`//` divides and throws away anything after the decimal point. 7 // 2 is 3.
symbols: divide and drop the decimal part

example.caption: Check the remainder column. Even numbers leave 0 when divided by 2.

predict.why: 4 goes into 10 twice (8) leaving 2, so 10 % 4 is 2 and 10 // 4 is 2. 12 divides exactly by 4, so 12 % 4 is 0.

title: Making choices with if and else
idea: An `if` line asks a yes or no question. If the answer is True, Python runs the indented lines under it. If False, it skips them.
`else` is the plan B. It runs only when the `if` question was False. `elif` means else if: another question, asked only when the earlier ones were False.
The colon `:` at the end of the line and the indent (4 spaces) are required. The indent shows which lines belong to the choice.
symbols: ends the line and says the indented lines below belong to it
run the lines below only when the question is True
else if: another question, asked only if the earlier ones were False
run the lines below when nothing above was True

example.caption: Follow which lines get highlighted. Lines inside a choice that was not taken are skipped.

predict.why: n > 5 is False, so A is skipped. n > 1 is True, so B prints. After one choice is taken, the rest are skipped, so C does not print.

title: Lists: many values in one name
idea: A list holds several values in order, written inside square brackets with commas between them.
Each value sits in its own box, and each box has a number called its position (also called its index). The first box is position 0, not 1.
`append` adds a new value to the end of the list.
symbols: separates the values in a list
add one value to the end of a list

example.caption: Watch the row of boxes. Position numbers are shown above each box.

predict.why: append puts the new value at the end.

title: Indexing: picking one item by position
idea: To get one value out of a list, write the list name and the position in square brackets: `nums[0]` is the first value.
Positions start at 0. A list with 4 items has positions 0, 1, 2, 3. There is no position 4.
Negative positions count from the end. `nums[-1]` is the last item and `nums[-2]` is the one before it.
Asking for a position that does not exist stops the program with an IndexError.
symbols: the item at position 2 (the third item)
you asked for a position the list does not have

visuals.title: nums = [10, 20, 30, 40]. Top row: position from the start. Bottom row: position from the end.

example.caption: Step through and check each answer against the position numbers in the picture.
example.code:
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40]
first = nums[0]
third = nums[2]
last = nums[-1]
print(first, third, last)

predict.why: Position 1 is the second box, which holds 6. Position -2 is second from the end, which holds 9.

title: Slicing: copying a piece of a list
idea: A slice copies a piece. Write `nums[a:b]`. It starts at position a and stops just before position b. The position b itself is not included.
A handy fact: `nums[a:b]` has exactly b - a items.
Leave a side empty to mean the edge: `nums[:3]` starts at the very beginning and `nums[2:]` goes to the very end. `nums[::-1]` is a reversed copy.
symbols: items from position a up to but not including position b
from the start up to but not including b
from position a to the end

visuals.title: nums = [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. The green boxes are nums[1:4]: positions 1, 2 and 3.

example.caption: See how the end position is left out of each slice.
example.code:
nums = [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]
a = nums[1:4]
b = nums[:2]
c = nums[3:]
d = nums[::-1]
print(a)
print(b)
print(c)

predict.why: nums[2:5] starts at position 2 (value 3) and stops before position 5, so it holds 3, 4, 5. nums[:2] is positions 0 and 1.

title: len and the last position
idea: `len(nums)` counts how many items are in the list. A list of 4 items has a length of 4.
Because positions start at 0, the last position is always `len(nums) - 1`. This is the heart of off-by-one mistakes: the length and the last position are different numbers.
Remember: for 4 items, length is 4, positions are 0 to 3, and the last position is 3.
symbols: being wrong by exactly 1, often by mixing up length and last position

visuals.title: nums has 4 items. len(nums) is 4. The last position is 3.

example.caption: Compare the two printed numbers. They always differ by 1.
example.code:
nums = [8, 6, 7, 5]
size = len(nums)
last_pos = len(nums) - 1
last_item = nums[last_pos]
print(size, last_pos, last_item)

predict.why: There are 3 items so len is 3. The last position is 3 - 1 = 2, which holds 6. Writing nums[len(nums)] would be an IndexError.

title: range: counting numbers
idea: `range(n)` makes the numbers 0, 1, 2 and so on up to n - 1. It stops just before n, so it gives exactly n numbers.
`range(a, b)` starts at a and stops just before b. `range(a, b, step)` jumps by step each time.
Same rule as slicing: the end number is never included. To see the numbers, wrap it in `list( )`.
symbols: start at a, jump by s, stop before b
turns the run of numbers into a list you can see

visuals.title: range(5) gives these 5 numbers. Five numbers, but the biggest is 4.

example.caption: Each printed list shows what range makes.
example.code:
a = list(range(4))
b = list(range(2, 6))
c = list(range(0, 10, 3))
print(a)
print(b)
print(c)

predict.why: range(3) is 0, 1, 2. range(1, 4) starts at 1 and stops before 4, so 1, 2, 3.

title: for loops: values versus positions
idea: A `for` loop repeats the indented lines. The name after `for` takes the next thing each time around.

There are two common shapes. Shape one, over values: `for x in nums:` gives you each item itself. Shape two, over positions: `for i in range(len(nums)):` gives you 0, 1, 2 and so on, and you write `nums[i]` to get the item.
Use shape one when you only need the items. Use shape two when you need to know where you are, or to look at neighbours like `nums[i + 1]`.
symbols: x is each item, one per round
i is each position, one per round

example.caption: Shape one, over values. The name x holds the item itself.
example.code:
nums = [5, 8, 3]
total = 0
for x in nums:
    total = total + x
print(total)

example2.caption: Shape two, over positions. The name i holds the position, so we write nums[i] to get the item. Watch the arrow move along the boxes.
example2.code:
nums = [5, 8, 3]
total = 0
for i in range(len(nums)):
    total = total + nums[i]
print(total)

predict.why: i is the position, not the item. A list of 2 items has positions 0 and 1. To print the items you would write print(nums[i]).

title: Functions and return
idea: A function is a named set of steps you can use again. You make one with `def`. The names in brackets are the inputs it receives, called parameters.
`return` sends an answer back to whoever used the function, and stops the function right there.
Printing and returning are different. Print shows something on the screen. Return hands a value back so other code can use it. HackerRank functions almost always return.
symbols: make a function called name that receives a and b
use the function, giving it 3 and 4

example.caption: The function does not run when it is defined. It runs on the line that uses it.
example.code:
def add(a, b):
    result = a + b
    return result

answer = add(3, 4)
print(answer)

predict.why: double(5) hands back 10, and then 10 + 1 is 11.

title: Reading input the HackerRank way
idea: On HackerRank, the test data does not live in your code. It arrives as typed lines. `input()` reads one line, always as text.

To turn text into a whole number use `int( )`. To read a line like `3 1 4` as a list of numbers, use `list(map(int, input().split()))`. Read it in pieces: `input()` gets the line, `.split()` cuts it at spaces into separate pieces of text, `int` turns each piece into a number, and `list` collects them.
The first line often tells you how many items follow. You usually read that line and then read the next one.
symbols: read one line of typing, as text
cut text into pieces at the spaces
turn text into a whole number
collect the results into a list

example.caption: Here the typed input is the two lines 3 and then 5 8 2. Watch how text becomes numbers.
example.code:
n = int(input())
line = input()
pieces = line.split()
nums = list(map(int, pieces))
print(n, nums)

predict.why: split cuts the text into pieces, but the pieces are still text, so they keep their quote marks. int would turn them into numbers.

title: Strings: text is a row of letters
idea: Text in Python is called a string. A string works like a list of letters: it has positions starting at 0, and you can index and slice it the same way.
`len(word)` counts the letters. `word[0]` is the first letter. `word[::-1]` is the word reversed.

Useful tools: `.upper()` makes capitals, `.lower()` makes small letters, and `in` asks whether one piece of text is inside another. You cannot change a letter in place, you build a new string instead.
symbols: is the letter a somewhere inside word

example.caption: The letters sit in boxes just like list items.
example.code:
word = "planet"
first = word[0]
last = word[-1]
part = word[1:4]
back = word[::-1]
print(first, last, part, back)

predict.code:
w = "code"
print(len(w))
print(w[1])
print("d" in w)
predict.why: code has 4 letters. Position 1 is the second letter, o. The letter d is inside code, so the answer is True.
